root.stem: A 24-year-old man is evaluated with his wife after 2 years of trying to conceive. He is 190 cm tall with long legs, sparse facial and body hair, and mild breast enlargement. His testes are small and firm, and he needed extra help with reading and language at school. Semen analysis shows no sperm. Serum testosterone is low, and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) are both high. A testicular biopsy shows hyalinized seminiferous tubules without germ cells and clusters of Leydig cells.
root.oneliner: 24M + infertility for 2 years + tall with long legs + sparse body hair + mild breast enlargement + small firm testes + reading and language difficulty + no sperm + low testosterone, high FSH and LH + hyalinized tubules, no germ cells, clustered Leydig cells
highlight: hyalinized seminiferous tubules without germ cells

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A sex chromosome disorder with an extra X in a phenotypic male. The clincher: **a tall man with small firm testes, breast enlargement, no sperm, and low testosterone with high FSH and LH**.

nodes.q: Which karyotype causes it?
nodes.note: One extra X chromosome. His biopsy (hyalinized tubules with no germ cells and clustered Leydig cells) is the classic picture that points to 47,XXY. Mosaic forms (46,XY/47,XXY) are milder and may keep some fertility.

nodes.q: Which error in gamete formation produces the extra X?
nodes.a: Nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes in meiosis
nodes.note: It can arise in either parent: the extra X comes from the mother or from the father in roughly equal numbers. Advanced maternal age raises the risk slightly.

nodes.q: How many Barr bodies are seen in a cheek-cell smear?
nodes.note: Barr bodies equal the number of X chromosomes minus one. A typical male has none and a typical female has one.

nodes.q: Why is his follicle-stimulating hormone high?
nodes.a: Damaged Sertoli cells make less inhibin B
nodes.note: Loss of inhibin B removes the brake on FSH. Leydig cell failure lowers testosterone, so LH rises too: hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (the testes, not the pituitary, are failing). High LH drives aromatase, so the estrogen-to-testosterone ratio rises and the breasts enlarge.

nodes.q: Why is he tall with long legs?
nodes.a: Late closure of the growth plates because of low sex hormones
nodes.note: The long bones keep growing, so the legs are long compared with the trunk (eunuchoid proportions). An extra copy of the SHOX gene on the extra X adds to the height.

nodes.q: Which cancer, usually seen in women, is far more common in him than in other men?
nodes.note: Linked to the high estrogen-to-testosterone ratio. Extragonadal germ cell tumors (for example in the mediastinum) are also more common. Osteoporosis, type 2 diabetes and venous thrombosis are further long-term risks.

nodes.q: Which treatment is started to restore secondary sex characteristics and protect bone?
nodes.note: Started at puberty. It does not restore fertility. Men who want children can try sperm retrieval from the testis with intracytoplasmic sperm injection.

nodes.q: His height could suggest 47,XYY syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Tall with **normal testes, normal testosterone and normal fertility**; severe acne, learning and behavior problems
Tall with **small firm testes, no sperm, low testosterone and high FSH and LH**

nodes.q: His small testes, absent sperm and breast enlargement could suggest 46,XX testicular disorder of sex development. How do you tell them apart?

split.a: 46,XX testicular disorder of sex development (46,XX male)
split.note: **Normal or short height**, with the SRY gene moved onto an X chromosome; otherwise the same small testes, azoospermia and high FSH and LH
**Tall with long legs, 47,XXY with one Barr body plus a Y**

nodes.note: The trap: the testes, sperm count and hormones look the same; height and the karyotype separate them.

nodes.q: His breast enlargement and sparse body hair could suggest androgen insensitivity syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: 46,XY with **female external genitalia, a blind vagina, no uterus, and high testosterone and LH**
**Male external genitalia with small firm testes and low testosterone**

nodes.q: His small testes could suggest 45,X/46,XY mosaicism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Ambiguous genitalia, a streak gonad on one side and a testis on the other**, short stature, Turner-like features
**Normal male genitalia, tall stature, and two small firm testes**

nodes.q: His low testosterone could suggest hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low testosterone with low FSH and LH**; often anosmia (Kallmann syndrome); biopsy shows immature, not scarred, tubules
**Low testosterone with high FSH and LH**; hyalinized tubules

root.stem: A newborn boy has a gap in the left side of his upper lip that runs up into the left nostril, and the roof of his mouth is also open. He cannot form a seal around the nipple and milk comes out of his nose during feeding. His jaw is normal in size. He has no other malformations, his parents are unrelated, and there is no family history of birth defects.
root.oneliner: Newborn boy + gap in left upper lip into the nostril + open roof of the mouth + cannot seal on the nipple, milk from the nose + normal jaw + no other malformations + unrelated parents, no family history
highlight: gap in the left side of his upper lip
roof of his mouth is also open
milk comes out of his nose
no family history of birth defects

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A failure of the facial tissues to join in the embryo. The clincher: **a gap in the upper lip to one side of the midline, with an open palate and milk coming out of the nose**.

nodes.q: Which two structures failed to fuse to cause the cleft lip?
nodes.a: The maxillary prominence and the medial nasal prominence
nodes.note: They normally fuse in weeks 4 to 7, so the cleft sits to one side of the philtrum. The lateral nasal prominence forms the side of the nose and is not part of the upper lip fusion.

nodes.q: The two medial nasal prominences merge in the midline. Which structure do they form?
nodes.note: It gives the philtrum of the upper lip, the four upper incisor teeth and the primary palate. A cleft lip lies where the maxillary prominence fails to meet it.

nodes.q: Which structures failed to fuse to cause the open palate?
nodes.a: The lateral palatine processes, which fail to meet each other and the nasal septum
nodes.note: The palate closes later than the lip (by about week 12), which is why the lip and palate can be involved separately.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern best explains an isolated cleft in a healthy boy with unrelated parents and no family history?
nodes.note: Many genes plus environment (maternal smoking, alcohol, phenytoin, folate deficiency). The recurrence risk after one affected child is a few percent, much higher than the general population but far below a single-gene disease.

nodes.q: Which ear problem is common when the palate is open?
nodes.a: Recurrent middle ear infection with fluid (otitis media with effusion)
nodes.note: The tensor veli palatini, which opens the eustachian tube, works poorly when the palate is split, so fluid stays in the middle ear.

nodes.q: What can this fluid cause that delays his speech?
nodes.note: Speech problems also come from air escaping through the nose (hypernasal speech) and are treated by speech therapy.

nodes.q: At about what age is the cleft lip repaired?
nodes.note: The palate is closed later, at about 6 to 12 months, before speech develops. Care is by a team (surgeon, feeding specialist, audiologist, speech therapist, dentist). Special bottles help feeding until the palate is closed.

nodes.q: Clefts also occur in trisomy 13. How do you tell it from his isolated cleft?

split.note: **Cleft lip and palate with holoprosencephaly, extra fingers, small eyes and scalp defects**; severe intellectual disability and death in infancy
**Clefting with no other malformations and a normal karyotype**

nodes.note: The trap: trisomy 13 is the classic chromosome disorder with cleft lip and palate.

nodes.q: His feeding trouble could suggest Pierre Robin sequence. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small receding jaw, tongue falling back, and a U-shaped cleft of the palate only**; airway obstruction; no cleft lip
**Cleft of the lip to one side, with a normal-sized jaw**

nodes.q: A cleft can also run in families. How do you tell it from the autosomal dominant Van der Woude syndrome?

split.note: **Pits in the lower lip plus cleft lip or palate, passed from a parent** (IRF6 gene)
**No lip pits and no family history**

root.stem: A 5-month-old girl has had poor feeding and irritability since age 1 month and now flops over when she is placed to sit. Her head circumference is at the 3rd percentile. She has horizontal nystagmus, low trunk tone, brisk reflexes, sustained ankle clonus and upgoing toes on both sides. Blood lactate is high, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows symmetric lesions in the basal ganglia and brainstem. Respiratory chain studies on cultured skin fibroblasts show low complex II activity. Her parents are healthy and are first cousins.
root.oneliner: 5F + poor feeding and irritability since 1 month + flops when sitting + small head + horizontal nystagmus + low trunk tone, brisk reflexes, ankle clonus, bilateral upgoing toes + high lactate + symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions on MRI + low complex II activity + healthy parents who are first cousins
highlight: symmetric lesions in the basal ganglia and brainstem

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A mitochondrial disease of infants. The clincher: **an infant with low tone, nystagmus and upper motor neuron signs, high lactate, and symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions on MRI**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which cellular process fails?
nodes.note: Less ATP is made, so the tissues with the highest energy demand (brain, muscle) fail first. Complex I and complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) defects are the most common; complex II defects are rarer.

nodes.q: Which reaction does the deficient complex II carry out?
nodes.note: Complex II is succinate dehydrogenase: it passes the electrons (through FAD) to coenzyme Q and, unlike complexes I, III and IV, does not pump protons. It is the only enzyme that works in both the citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain. Do not confuse it with complex I (electrons from NADH to coenzyme Q) or complex III (electrons from ubiquinol to cytochrome c).

nodes.q: Why is her blood lactate high?
nodes.a: NADH builds up, so pyruvate is turned into lactate
nodes.note: With the chain blocked, NADH cannot be reoxidized, pyruvate is not burned in the citric acid cycle, and anaerobic glycolysis makes lactate.

nodes.q: What do the brain lesions show under the microscope?
nodes.a: Symmetric necrosis with spongy change, new capillaries and gliosis
nodes.note: The basal ganglia, thalamus and brainstem are most affected.

nodes.q: Every subunit of complex II is encoded in the nucleus. Which inheritance pattern fits her disease?
nodes.note: Complex II is the only respiratory chain complex with no subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Healthy first-cousin parents fit two carriers.

nodes.q: In other children, Leigh syndrome comes from a mutation in mitochondrial DNA. From which parent is such a mutation inherited?
nodes.note: Mitochondria come from the egg; sperm mitochondria are destroyed after fertilization. An affected mother passes it to all her children; an affected father to none.

nodes.q: Why can such a mother be almost well while her child is severely affected?
nodes.note: Each cell holds a mixture of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA, and the proportion varies between mother and child. A child who receives a high fraction of mutant DNA passes the threshold for disease.

nodes.q: A mutation in a mitochondrial transfer RNA gene can cause it. Why do mitochondria encode their own transfer RNAs?
nodes.a: Mitochondria use a non-standard genetic code
nodes.note: For example UGA codes for tryptophan instead of stop, and AUA codes for methionine, so cytoplasmic transfer RNAs cannot read mitochondrial messages.

nodes.q: Which event usually ends her life?
nodes.note: Death is usually in early childhood.

nodes.q: Which treatment is available?
nodes.a: Supportive care with mitochondrial cofactors such as thiamine and coenzyme Q10
nodes.note: There is no cure. Valproate should be avoided in mitochondrial disease.

nodes.q: Her high lactate could suggest mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Onset in childhood or early adult life; **stroke-like episodes that do not follow a vessel territory**, seizures, migraine, hearing loss
Onset in **infancy with nystagmus, low tone, and basal ganglia and brainstem lesions**

nodes.note: The trap: both are mitochondrial diseases with high lactate, and both can involve mitochondrial transfer RNA mutations.

nodes.q: Her irritability and poor head control could suggest Krabbe disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Irritability, **stiffness, optic atrophy and absent reflexes from nerve damage**, globoid cells; galactocerebrosidase deficiency; **normal lactate**
**High lactate, nystagmus, and brisk reflexes with basal ganglia lesions**

nodes.q: Her floppiness could suggest Werdnig-Hoffmann disease (spinal muscular atrophy type 1). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Alert child with **tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes** (lower motor neuron); survival motor neuron 1 (SMN1) gene deletion
**Brisk reflexes, ankle clonus, upgoing toes and nystagmus** (upper motor neuron and brainstem)

root.stem: A newborn girl has downward-slanting eyes with a notch in the outer part of both lower eyelids, underdeveloped cheekbones, a very small lower jaw, and small, misshapen ears with narrow ear canals. She breathes noisily when lying on her back and fails her hearing screen. Her thumbs and hands are normal, and her father has similar but milder facial features.
root.oneliner: Newborn girl + downward-slanting eyes + notch in both lower eyelids + flat cheekbones + very small jaw + small malformed ears, narrow canals + noisy breathing supine + fails hearing screen + normal thumbs and hands + father mildly affected
highlight: notch in the outer part of both lower eyelids
her father has similar but milder facial features

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A disorder of facial bone and ear development. The clincher: **downward-slanting eyes with lower eyelid notches, flat cheekbones, a tiny jaw, malformed ears and hearing loss, with normal hands**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which pharyngeal arch fails to form properly?
nodes.note: The first arch gives the mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, malleus, incus and the muscles of mastication; its nerve is the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve.

nodes.q: Which embryonic cell population fails to reach the arch in enough numbers?
nodes.note: A defect in the TCOF1 gene (treacle, needed to make ribosomes) causes these cells to die before they migrate.

nodes.q: Which middle ear bone, attached to the eardrum, comes from the same arch as her jaw?
nodes.note: The malleus (with the incus) comes from the first arch (Meckel cartilage). The stapes comes from the second arch, the greater horn of the hyoid from the third, the thyroid cartilage from the fourth, and the cricoid from the sixth.

nodes.q: Which type of hearing loss follows?
nodes.note: Malformed ossicles and narrow or absent ear canals block sound before it reaches the cochlea. Bone-conduction hearing aids help.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern fits her father's milder features?
nodes.note: Many cases are new mutations with no family history. Intelligence is usually normal.

nodes.q: Which early problem can be fatal?
nodes.note: A small jaw lets the tongue fall back, and the airway is narrow.

nodes.q: What is the first management priority?
nodes.a: Securing the airway (prone positioning, then tracheostomy if needed)
nodes.note: Later: feeding support, hearing devices, and staged reconstruction of the jaw, cheekbones and ears.

nodes.q: Her tiny jaw and noisy breathing could suggest Pierre Robin sequence. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small jaw, tongue falling back and a U-shaped cleft palate**; normal eyes, cheekbones and ears
**Eyelid notches, flat cheekbones and malformed ears** along with the small jaw; palate often normal

nodes.note: The trap: both have a small mandible from first arch maldevelopment.

nodes.q: Her ear and jaw anomalies could suggest DiGeorge syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low calcium with seizures, congenital heart disease of the outflow tract, and absent thymus with T cell deficiency**; 22q11.2 deletion
**Eyelid notches and flat cheekbones with normal heart, calcium and immunity**

nodes.q: Her ear anomalies could suggest Goldenhar syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Usually **one-sided**, with an eye growth on the cornea (epibulbar dermoid) and **vertebral anomalies**
**Both sides equally affected, with lower eyelid notches** and normal spine

root.stem: A newborn boy has no visible iris in either eye, so the pupils look very large and black, and his eyes drift in a jerky, wandering pattern. His father and several paternal relatives have the same eye finding and poor vision since childhood. His genitalia are normal and abdominal ultrasonography shows no mass. Chromosome analysis shows the same balanced translocation involving the short arm of chromosome 11 in him, his father and every affected relative, and in none of the unaffected relatives. The translocation breakpoint lies outside the coding region of the eye development gene.
root.oneliner: Newborn boy + no visible iris in either eye, huge black pupils + jerky wandering eye movements + father and paternal relatives affected + normal genitalia + no abdominal mass + same balanced 11p translocation in all affected relatives, breakpoint outside the gene's coding region
highlight: no visible iris in either eye

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Congenital absence of most of the iris. The clincher: **no visible iris from birth in both eyes, with nystagmus and an affected parent**.

nodes.q: Which gene is affected?
nodes.note: At 11p13. It encodes a transcription factor that directs eye development.

nodes.q: Why is one working copy not enough?
nodes.note: Half the normal amount of PAX6 protein is too little to form the iris and the fovea.

nodes.q: The translocation breakpoint lies outside PAX6's coding sequence. How does it still cause disease?
nodes.a: It disrupts a regulatory sequence of the gene (position effect), so PAX6 is not expressed properly
nodes.note: The gene itself is intact, but its enhancer is cut off from it. This is not a new stop codon, a missing intron, a skipped exon or a base change.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern fits his family?
nodes.note: About two thirds of cases are inherited and one third are new mutations.

nodes.q: What causes his jerky eye movements and poor vision from birth?
nodes.note: The macula does not develop normally, so the eyes cannot fix on a target.

nodes.q: Which pressure-related eye complication threatens vision later in childhood?
nodes.note: Cataract and corneal clouding (from limbal stem cell failure) are also common.

nodes.q: Which test is done in a child with new (sporadic) aniridia?
nodes.a: Chromosome microarray or FISH for an 11p13 deletion
nodes.note: A deletion that includes the neighbouring WT1 gene carries a high risk of Wilms tumor; if present, abdominal ultrasonography is repeated about every 3 months until about age 8.

nodes.q: His aniridia could be part of WAGR syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: New **11p13 deletion including WT1 and PAX6**: Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies and a Range of developmental delay
**Inherited from the father, normal genitalia and kidneys, and only the PAX6 regulatory region disrupted**

nodes.note: The trap: both lack an iris because PAX6 is lost; the neighbouring WT1 deletion is what adds Wilms tumor.

nodes.q: His large black pupils could suggest an iris coloboma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Keyhole-shaped pupil with a notch at the bottom** and usually one eye; part of the iris is present
**Both irises almost completely absent**, with nystagmus

root.stem: An 18-year-old woman has had pale, greasy, foul-smelling stools since infancy. For 2 years she has had clumsy movements of her arms and legs, and she now has trouble seeing in dim light. Her 16-year-old brother has similar symptoms, and both parents are healthy with normal cholesterol levels. She has ataxia, absent deep tendon reflexes and loss of position sense. Fundoscopy shows pigmentary retinopathy, a blood smear shows red cells with spiny projections, and her total cholesterol is 40 mg/dL.
root.oneliner: 18F + greasy foul stools since infancy + 2 years of clumsy limb movements + poor vision in dim light + brother affected, parents healthy with normal cholesterol + ataxia, absent reflexes, lost position sense + pigmentary retinopathy + spiny red cells + total cholesterol 40 mg/dL
highlight: both parents are healthy with normal cholesterol levels

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A failure to make lipoproteins that carry fat out of the gut and liver. The clincher: **fat malabsorption from infancy + ataxia and retinal degeneration + spiny red cells + very low cholesterol**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which apolipoprotein is missing from the blood?
nodes.note: Without apolipoprotein B there are no chylomicrons, very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) or low-density lipoprotein (LDL), so blood cholesterol and triglycerides are very low.

nodes.q: Which defective protein is the actual cause?
nodes.note: MTP loads fat onto apolipoprotein B inside the endoplasmic reticulum; without it the apolipoprotein cannot be exported. Autosomal recessive (MTTP gene), which fits her healthy parents and affected brother.

nodes.q: What does an intestinal biopsy after a fatty meal show?
nodes.a: Enterocytes packed with fat droplets, with normal villi
nodes.note: Fat gets into the cell but cannot leave it as chylomicrons.

nodes.q: Why do her red cells have spiny projections?
nodes.a: Abnormal lipid composition of the red cell membrane
nodes.note: These cells are called acanthocytes.

nodes.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes her ataxia, absent reflexes and loss of position sense?
nodes.note: Vitamin E travels in chylomicrons and VLDL. Its lack damages the spinocerebellar tracts and the dorsal columns.

nodes.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes her trouble seeing in dim light?
nodes.note: Night blindness comes from lack of vitamin A for rhodopsin. The pigmentary retinopathy is driven mainly by vitamin E lack. Vitamin K lack can cause bleeding, and vitamin D lack bone disease.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: A low-fat diet with high-dose fat-soluble vitamins, above all vitamin E
nodes.note: Early treatment can prevent the nerve and eye damage.

nodes.q: Which drug for homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia works by inhibiting the same protein?
nodes.note: It copies this disease on purpose, lowering LDL, but can cause fatty liver and fat in the stool.

nodes.q: Her ataxia and absent reflexes could suggest Friedreich ataxia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: GAA repeat in the frataxin gene; **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, diabetes, foot deformity and scoliosis**; normal stools and normal cholesterol
**Greasy stools, spiny red cells and cholesterol of 40 mg/dL**, with retinal degeneration

nodes.note: The trap: both are autosomal recessive with ataxia, areflexia and lost position sense.

nodes.q: Her fatty stools since infancy could suggest cystic fibrosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Recurrent lung infections and high sweat chloride** with pancreatic insufficiency; normal cholesterol
**No lung disease, spiny red cells and very low cholesterol**

nodes.q: Low cholesterol could suggest familial hypobetalipoproteinemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Autosomal dominant APOB mutation; carriers have **low LDL, and are often well**
Autosomal recessive; **parents have normal cholesterol and the patient is severely ill**

root.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of 2 months of chest pain and shortness of breath when he climbs stairs. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 8 years. His father had a heart attack at age 44, and a paternal uncle died suddenly at age 39. He has firm yellow nodules over the extensor tendons of both hands, thickened Achilles tendons, and a pale gray ring around the edge of each cornea. Total cholesterol is 380 mg/dL, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is 300 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol is 40 mg/dL, and triglycerides are 120 mg/dL. Thyroid function tests are normal and he takes no medications.
root.oneliner: 27M + exertional chest pain and dyspnea + smoker + father with heart attack at 44, uncle died suddenly at 39 + yellow nodules on hand tendons, thick Achilles tendons + corneal ring + total cholesterol 380, LDL 300, HDL 40, triglycerides 120 + normal thyroid tests
highlight: chest pain and shortness of breath when he climbs stairs
father had a heart attack at age 44
firm yellow nodules over the extensor tendons of both hands
pale gray ring around the edge of each cornea

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A genetic disorder of cholesterol clearance. The clincher: **tendon xanthomas + very high LDL cholesterol with normal triglycerides + early heart disease in relatives**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The exam uses both names for the same disease: raised LDL with normal very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) and triglycerides.

nodes.q: What is the pattern of inheritance?
nodes.note: One faulty copy (heterozygote) roughly doubles LDL cholesterol and brings heart disease in the 30s to 50s; two faulty copies (homozygote) give levels above 600 mg/dL and heart attacks in childhood.

nodes.q: Which hepatic protein is deficient or defective?
nodes.note: The liver clears LDL from the blood through this receptor, so a defect means **decreased clearance of LDL by the liver**, not overproduction or increased absorption. Blood LDL stays high and cholesterol is deposited in tissues. Rarer causes of the same picture: defective apolipoprotein B-100 or gain-of-function PCSK9.

nodes.q: Which apolipoprotein on the LDL particle binds this receptor?
nodes.note: Apolipoprotein B-48 is on chylomicrons and does not bind the LDL receptor; apolipoprotein E binds the remnant receptor.

nodes.q: Where on the hepatocyte surface is the LDL receptor taken into the cell?
nodes.note: The receptor-LDL complex enters by receptor-mediated endocytosis; the vesicle fuses with a lysosome, the receptor is recycled and the cholesterol is released.

nodes.q: A cell binds LDL with normal affinity but cannot take it in, while it takes up transferrin normally. Which part of the receptor is mutated?
nodes.a: The cytoplasmic domain (tail) of the LDL receptor
nodes.note: Normal transferrin uptake shows the clathrin pits themselves work. The tail carries the signal that recruits clathrin to the receptor. A defect in the extracellular domain would instead stop LDL binding.

nodes.q: What fills the yellow nodules on his tendons?
nodes.note: Cholesterol esters deposit in tendons (xanthomas), in the eyelids (xanthelasma) and at the corneal edge (corneal arcus), which is abnormal in a man under 45.

nodes.q: Which vessel disease develops early in his life?
Which event is the main cause of death?
nodes.note: Lipid-laden plaques narrow or rupture in the coronary arteries; untreated homozygotes may die in childhood or the teens.

nodes.q: After his lipid panel, how are other affected people in his family found?
nodes.a: Cascade screening: lipid testing (and genetic testing) of his first-degree relatives
nodes.note: Test children of an affected parent early (from about age 2). Rule out secondary causes of high LDL first, such as hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome and cholestasis.

nodes.q: Which drug class is first-line, started at a high dose?
nodes.note: They block 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis. Add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor) if LDL stays high; homozygotes may need LDL apheresis.

nodes.q: In a heterozygote, which hepatic protein is upregulated by a drug that inhibits cholesterol synthesis?
nodes.note: Falling cell cholesterol activates sterol regulatory element-binding protein, so the liver makes more receptors from its normal allele and clears more LDL. Homozygotes with no working receptors respond poorly.

nodes.q: Which add-on drug class raises the number of LDL receptors by stopping their breakdown in lysosomes?
nodes.note: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) binds the LDL receptor and sends it to the lysosome; monoclonal antibodies against it let the receptor recycle. Ezetimibe instead blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1).

nodes.q: His family history could suggest familial defective apolipoprotein B-100. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Looks the same at the bedside; the **LDL receptor is normal but apolipoprotein B-100 on the LDL particle binds it poorly**, found on genetic testing; usually milder
**Defective or missing LDL receptor** with tendon xanthomas, LDL 300 and normal triglycerides

nodes.note: The trap: both are autosomal dominant with tendon xanthomas and early heart disease, but the faulty protein is on different sides of the receptor-ligand pair.

nodes.q: His blood lipids could suggest familial hypertriglyceridemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised triglycerides and VLDL with normal or low LDL**; recurrent pancreatitis, no tendon xanthomas
**LDL 300 with normal triglycerides + tendon xanthomas**

nodes.note: An affected mother passes the mutation to all of her children; an affected father passes it to none, because sperm mitochondria are not passed on at fertilization. Here all her siblings are affected and her father's side is healthy.

nodes.q: Why do affected relatives differ in severity?
nodes.note: Cells hold a mixture of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA; the proportion in each tissue sets the disease.

nodes.q: Which cellular process fails, as shown by the muscle stain?

nodes.note: Without a working respiratory chain, the cell cannot oxidize NADH.

nodes.q: What has piled up beneath the cell membrane of the ragged red fibers?
nodes.note: The fibers look ragged and red on modified Gomori trichrome stain because the cell makes more (faulty) mitochondria to make up for the energy failure.

nodes.note: Cystine builds up and crystallizes inside lysosomes of the kidney, cornea, bone marrow, thyroid and muscle.

nodes.note: Both parents are healthy carriers.

nodes.note: Of the three unaffected outcomes of two carrier parents, two are carriers (and one is homozygous normal); the affected outcome is excluded.

nodes.note: Fetal infection with rubella virus (German measles) in early pregnancy. The clincher: **cataracts + patent ductus arteriosus or pulmonary artery stenosis + sensorineural deafness after a first-trimester maternal rash with postauricular nodes**.

nodes.q: What kind of virus causes it?
nodes.a: An enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus (rubella virus)
nodes.note: Now classed in the genus Rubivirus (family Matonaviridae); older books list it as a togavirus. It spreads by respiratory droplets and crosses the placenta during maternal viremia.

nodes.q: Which lymph node groups were enlarged in the mother?
nodes.note: The mild rash, arthralgia and these nodes are typical of maternal rubella; up to half of infections are subclinical.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability. The clincher: **a floppy newborn with upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat face, a single palmar crease and a sandal gap, born to an older mother whose quadruple screen showed low AFP and estriol with high hCG and inhibin A**. Karyotype confirms it.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?

nodes.q: Which chromosomal event causes most cases?

nodes.q: In which meiotic division does the error usually happen?
nodes.note: Homologous chromosomes 21 fail to separate in the egg, which has been arrested in prophase I since the mother's own fetal life; this is why age matters.

nodes.q: Which type of translocation does his aunt carry?
nodes.note: The long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes (here 14 and 21) fuse and the short arms are lost, so a balanced carrier has 45 chromosomes and is healthy. About 4% of Down syndrome comes from an unbalanced form (46 chromosomes with the extra 21q attached to 14), which is not related to maternal age. A female carrier's risk of an affected child is about 10-15% (lower if the father carries it); a 21;21 carrier can only have affected or miscarried pregnancies.

nodes.q: Which test gives her fetus's karyotype now, at 12 weeks?

nodes.q: Which first-trimester combined-test pattern would have flagged the pregnancy earlier?

nodes.note: Done at 11-14 weeks. Nuchal translucency is fluid behind the fetal neck (also thick in heart defects and Turner syndrome). Low PAPP-A with LOW hCG points instead to trisomy 18 or 13. nodes.q: Which congenital heart defect is most common?

nodes.q: Which gut malformation explains the bilious vomiting and the two gas bubbles?

nodes.q: Which cancer group is raised 10-20 fold in childhood?
nodes.note: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common type; acute megakaryoblastic leukemia is typical before age 5, often after a transient abnormal myelopoiesis in the newborn (GATA1 mutation).

nodes.q: Which brain disease appears by middle age in almost all affected adults?
nodes.note: The amyloid precursor protein gene lies on chromosome 21, so three copies give extra beta-amyloid; plaques appear by age 40.

nodes.q: His heart defect, low AFP and estriol, and his mother's age could also suggest Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18). How do you tell them apart?

root.stem: A 6-year-old boy has had 7 fractures after minor falls, and each healed quickly without deformity. The whites of both eyes look blue-gray, he has mild hearing loss, his joints are unusually loose, and he bruises easily, but his skin is not stretchy. His teeth are translucent and wear down quickly. A scrape on his knee healed with a wide, thin scar. His father also has blue-gray whites of the eyes and hearing loss, and the boy's vitamin D level is normal.
root.oneliner: 6M + 7 fractures after minor falls, healing fast + blue-gray sclerae + mild hearing loss + loose joints, easy bruising, skin not stretchy + translucent teeth + wide thin scar + father with blue-gray sclerae and hearing loss + normal vitamin D
highlight: His father also has blue-gray whites of the eyes and hearing loss

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A disorder of type I collagen. The clincher: **repeated fractures from minor trauma + blue sclerae + hearing loss, in a family**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: A defect in the synthesis of which compound explains the fractures?
nodes.note: Mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2. The mild form (type I) usually makes too little normal type I collagen; severe forms carry glycine substitutions that disrupt the triple helix. Hydroxyproline is only an amino acid in collagen, and hydroxyapatite is the bone mineral, which is made normally.

nodes.q: How is his disease most likely inherited?
nodes.note: His father is affected too. Rarer severe forms are autosomal recessive.

nodes.q: Why do his sclerae look blue-gray?
nodes.a: The sclera is thin from too little type I collagen, so the dark choroid shows through
nodes.note: Type I collagen is the main protein of bone, tendon, skin, sclera and dentin.

nodes.q: Which part of wound healing is most directly affected?
nodes.note: Granulation tissue first fills the wound with type III collagen, which is replaced by type I collagen to form the scar. With too little type I collagen the scar is thin and weak. Clotting, inflammation and cell migration are normal.

nodes.q: Which kind of hearing loss develops?
nodes.note: The ossicles are abnormal, as in otosclerosis; sensorineural loss may be added in adults.

nodes.q: What is the dental defect called?
nodes.note: Dentin is rich in type I collagen, so the teeth look opalescent and wear down quickly.

nodes.q: Which drug class lowers his fracture rate?
nodes.note: They inhibit osteoclast bone resorption. Pamidronate or zoledronic acid is given intravenously in children; physiotherapy and rod placement in long bones also help.

nodes.q: Repeated fractures in a child could suggest child abuse. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fractures in different stages of healing + posterior rib or metaphyseal corner fractures + history that does not fit**; white sclerae, no family history
**Blue sclerae + hearing loss + family history + translucent teeth**; fractures after minor trauma

nodes.note: The trap: both give repeated fractures in a child and bruising, and the two can coexist.

nodes.q: His loose joints and easy bruising could suggest Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hyperextensible, fragile skin + hypermobile joints**; defect in type V or type III collagen; fractures are not the problem
**Many fractures + blue sclerae + hearing loss**; the skin is not stretchy

nodes.q: His loose joints could suggest Marfan syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tall, long limbs + upward lens dislocation + aortic root dilation**; fibrillin-1 defect; bones are not brittle
**Many fractures + blue sclerae + hearing loss + translucent teeth**; bones are brittle, not long

nodes.q: Fractures in a child could suggest vitamin D deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bowed legs, widened wrists, beaded ribs; low vitamin D, high PTH and alkaline phosphatase**; normal sclerae
**Blue sclerae + hearing loss + family history**; normal vitamin D

root.stem: A 3-month-old boy is brought in because of yellow skin and eyes and poor movement since birth. He is floppy with a high forehead, a flat midface and wide-open anterior and posterior fontanelles. His liver is enlarged, direct bilirubin and liver enzymes are raised, and he has had seizures. Serum very-long-chain fatty acids are markedly raised. A liver biopsy shows foamy, fat-filled hepatocytes with cell death. His older sister died at 5 months with a similar illness, and both parents are healthy.
root.oneliner: 3-month-old M + jaundice, floppy since birth + high forehead, flat midface, wide-open fontanelles + enlarged liver, direct bilirubin up + seizures + very-long-chain fatty acids up + foamy hepatocytes with cell death + older sister died at 5 months, healthy parents
highlight: Serum very-long-chain fatty acids are markedly raised

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most severe peroxisomal biogenesis disorder. The clincher: **a floppy infant with a flat face, large fontanelles, an enlarged liver and raised very-long-chain fatty acids**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease; it is the severe end of the Zellweger spectrum.

nodes.q: Which organelle is missing or nonfunctional in his liver cells?
nodes.note: Unlike lysosomal diseases, the cells lack the organelle itself; the other organelles (Golgi, mitochondria, smooth endoplasmic reticulum) are present.

nodes.q: Which defect caused by mutations in the PEX (peroxin) genes leads to this?
nodes.a: Failure to import enzymes into the peroxisome
nodes.note: Autosomal recessive, which fits his healthy parents and affected sibling. Enzymes are made but cannot enter, so all peroxisomal functions fail.

nodes.q: Which peroxisomal process fails so that very-long-chain fatty acids accumulate?
nodes.note: Also lost: plasmalogen synthesis (needed for myelin), bile acid synthesis and phytanic acid breakdown. Very-long-chain fatty acids build up in liver and brain. Raised plasma levels are the first test, then PEX gene testing.

nodes.q: Which brain finding explains the seizures and floppiness?
nodes.note: The cortex is abnormally layered (polymicrogyria), and myelin is also lost because plasmalogens are not made. The child also has kidney cysts and calcific stippling of the patella and cartilage.

nodes.q: What is the usual outcome?
nodes.note: There is no cure; care is supportive.

nodes.q: His jaundice could suggest biliary atresia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pale stools + dark urine in a baby with normal tone, normal fontanelles and normal very-long-chain fatty acids**; improved by an early Kasai procedure
**Floppy + large fontanelles + flat face + seizures + raised very-long-chain fatty acids**

nodes.note: The trap: both give jaundice with direct bilirubin and an enlarged liver in a young infant.

nodes.q: His enlarged liver and floppiness could suggest a lysosomal storage disease such as Gaucher disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Vacuolated cells filled with undigested substrate from one missing lysosomal enzyme** (Gaucher: crumpled-tissue-paper macrophages, big spleen, bone pain); normal very-long-chain fatty acids
**No peroxisomes + raised very-long-chain fatty acids + large fontanelles**

nodes.q: Raised very-long-chain fatty acids occur in another peroxisomal disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Boy aged 4-10 with school decline, adrenal insufficiency and cerebral demyelination; ABCD1 transporter defect**; peroxisomes are present
**Newborn with severe floppiness, flat face, large fontanelles and absent peroxisomes**; autosomal recessive

root.stem: A newborn girl is delivered at 39 weeks to a 41-year-old woman. She has a small head, a cleft lip and palate, an extra finger beside the fifth finger on each hand, a scalp skin defect, and very small eyes set close together. A harsh holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border, and a head MRI shows the cerebral hemispheres have not separated into two halves.
root.oneliner: Newborn F + 41-year-old mother + small head, cleft lip and palate + extra finger beside the fifth + scalp defect + small close-set eyes + holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border + hemispheres not separated on MRI
highlight: extra finger beside the fifth finger
very small eyes set close together

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Trisomy 13. The clincher: **a newborn with holoprosencephaly, midline facial clefts, extra fingers and a scalp defect, born to an older mother**. Karyotype confirms it.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which brain malformation explains the small head and facial clefts?
nodes.note: The forebrain fails to split into two hemispheres; the more severe the brain defect, the more severe the midline face defect, up to cyclopia.

nodes.q: Which signaling pathway drives the midline patterning that failed here?
nodes.note: Sonic hedgehog from the prechordal plate patterns the midline forebrain and face; its failure gives holoprosencephaly, close-set eyes and midline clefts.

nodes.q: Which chromosomal event causes most cases?
nodes.note: The risk rises with maternal age. A minority arise from a Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 13.

nodes.q: Which heart defect most likely explains her murmur?
nodes.note: Heart defects occur in about 80%; atrial septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus are also common.

nodes.q: What is the extra finger beside the fifth finger called?
nodes.note: An extra digit on the ulnar side of the hand. Rocker-bottom feet occur in trisomy 13 and in trisomy 18.

nodes.q: What is the usual outcome?
nodes.a: Death in the first year of life (most within days to weeks)
nodes.note: Care is supportive and decisions are made with the parents.

nodes.q: Her heart defect and her mother's age could suggest Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Clenched fists with overlapping fingers + rocker-bottom feet + small jaw + prominent back of the head**; no midline cleft or holoprosencephaly
**Holoprosencephaly + cleft lip and palate + extra fingers + scalp defect**

nodes.note: The trap: both are lethal trisomies of older mothers with heart defects and small size.

nodes.q: A trisomy in a baby of an older mother could suggest Down syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Floppy + upslanting eyes + sandal gap + single palmar crease**; survives to adulthood; hCG and inhibin A high
**Small head + midline clefts + holoprosencephaly + extra fingers**; survival beyond the first year is rare

nodes.note: On first-trimester screening, hCG is high in Down syndrome but low in trisomies 13 and 18 (PAPP-A is low in all three).

nodes.q: Holoprosencephaly can occur without a trisomy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal karyotype; sonic hedgehog (SHH) gene mutation or maternal diabetes**; no extra fingers or scalp defect
**Holoprosencephaly + extra fingers + scalp defect**; karyotype shows an extra chromosome 13

root.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought in because he eats constantly and has gained a lot of weight. He was floppy and fed poorly as an infant. He is short, has an intellectual disability, almond-shaped eyes and small genitalia with undescended testes. He has been found taking food from the trash. Karyotype is normal and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for a deletion at 15q11-q13 is normal.
root.oneliner: 5M + constant eating, weight gain + floppy, poor feeding as an infant + short, intellectual disability + almond-shaped eyes + small genitalia, undescended testes + normal karyotype, normal FISH at 15q11-q13
highlight: floppy and fed poorly as an infant
FISH) for a deletion at 15q11-q13 is normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An imprinting disorder. The clincher: **infant hypotonia and poor feeding followed by constant hunger and obesity, small genitalia and intellectual disability**.

nodes.q: Which parent's copy of 15q11-q13 is missing or not expressed?
nodes.note: The maternal copy is normally silenced by imprinting (methylation), so losing the paternal copy leaves no working genes in the region.

nodes.q: His FISH test shows no deletion. Which finding most likely confirms the disease?
nodes.a: Maternal uniparental disomy (both chromosomes 15 from his mother)
nodes.note: Two maternal copies means no paternal copy is expressed. It usually arises when a trisomy 15 conceptus loses the paternal chromosome. Deletion of the paternal chromosome (about 70%) is the commonest cause, and an imprinting-center defect is rare.

nodes.q: Which test finds all of these causes?
nodes.note: FISH finds only a deletion, so a normal result does not exclude the disease.

nodes.q: Which part of the brain explains the constant hunger?
nodes.note: Hypothalamic dysfunction gives hyperphagia, low sex hormones and poor growth hormone secretion; ghrelin is high.

nodes.q: Which metabolic disease does his obesity most often cause?
nodes.note: Also obstructive sleep apnea; obesity-related heart and lung failure is the leading cause of death, and binge eating can cause choking or gastric rupture.

nodes.q: Which hormone treatment is given to improve growth and body composition?
nodes.note: Plus strict calorie restriction and locked food storage, and sex hormone replacement at puberty.

nodes.q: The same region of chromosome 15 is involved in Angelman syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Happy puppet: severe speech delay, ataxia, seizures, inappropriate laughter**; missing maternal UBE3A
**Hypotonia then hyperphagia and obesity, small genitalia**; missing paternal genes

nodes.note: The trap: the same deletion causes either disease, depending on which parent it came from.

nodes.q: His obesity and intellectual disability could suggest Bardet-Biedl syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Obesity + retinitis pigmentosa + extra fingers + kidney anomalies**; a ciliopathy
**Infant hypotonia + hyperphagia + almond eyes + small genitalia**; imprinting

nodes.q: His intellectual disability and floppiness in infancy could suggest Down syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Upslanting eyes + sandal gap + single palmar crease**; extra chromosome 21 on karyotype
**Constant hunger + obesity + small genitalia**; normal karyotype

root.stem: A 15-year-old girl has grown 12 cm in the past year and has had palpitations. Her father is 190 cm tall. She has a long thin face, long thin fingers, an arm span greater than her height, a chest wall that is sunken in, and joints that bend unusually far. Eye examination shows the lens of each eye displaced upward. A mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur are heard at the apex, and echocardiography shows a dilated aortic root. Her skin is not stretchy, she has no intellectual disability, and her plasma homocysteine is normal.
root.oneliner: 15F + grew 12 cm in a year + palpitations + tall father + long thin face, long fingers, arm span > height, sunken chest, loose joints + lens displaced upward + mid-systolic click, late systolic murmur + dilated aortic root + normal skin, no intellectual disability, normal homocysteine
highlight: arm span greater than her height
mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A connective tissue disorder. The clincher: **tall with long limbs + upward lens dislocation + aortic root dilation**.

nodes.q: Which protein is defective?
nodes.note: Autosomal dominant mutation of the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15; about 25% are new mutations. Fibrillin-1 forms the microfibril scaffold for elastin and holds back TGF-beta, so extra TGF-beta signaling weakens tissues.

nodes.q: One mutation affecting eye, heart and skeleton is an example of which genetic principle?
nodes.note: A single gene produces effects in several organ systems. Heterogeneity means different genes cause the same disease, anticipation means worse disease in later generations, and polygenic inheritance involves many genes.

nodes.q: Which weakened structure lets her lenses slip upward?
nodes.a: The zonular fibers (suspensory ligament of the lens)
nodes.note: The zonules are made of fibrillin, so they stretch and the lens moves up and out (superotemporal).

nodes.q: Which valve lesion explains the click and late systolic murmur?
nodes.note: Myxomatous change of the leaflets.

nodes.q: Which aortic wall change underlies the aortic root dilation?
nodes.note: Loss of elastic fibers in the media weakens the wall.

nodes.q: Which event kills many untreated patients?
nodes.note: Dissection or rupture of the dilated ascending aorta, often into the pericardium, causing tamponade.

nodes.q: Which drug is used to slow aortic root growth because it also dampens TGF-beta signaling?
nodes.note: An angiotensin II receptor blocker; beta-blockers are the other standard choice and lower the force of ejection.

nodes.q: What is done when the aortic root reaches about 5 cm?
nodes.note: The root is followed with yearly echocardiography; surgery is done earlier if it grows quickly or a relative had a dissection. She should avoid heavy lifting and contact sports.

nodes.q: Her tall body and lens dislocation could suggest homocystinuria. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lens displaced down and in + intellectual disability + blood clots; high homocysteine** (cystathionine synthase deficiency); autosomal recessive
**Lens displaced up and out + aortic root dilation + normal intelligence**; autosomal dominant

nodes.note: The trap: both give a tall marfanoid habitus and lens dislocation.

nodes.q: Her joint hypermobility could suggest Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hyperextensible, fragile skin + easy bruising + joint hypermobility**; collagen defect
**Normal skin + tall + lens dislocation + aortic root dilation**

root.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had progressive coarsening of his face over the past year, with a large tongue, thick lips and increased body hair. His corneas look cloudy, his joints are stiff, and he has an umbilical hernia. His liver and spleen are enlarged and he has lost developmental milestones. X-rays show thickened ribs and beaked vertebrae. Urine tests show raised glycosaminoglycans. His blood thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal and his plasma lysosomal enzyme levels are normal.
root.oneliner: 3M + progressive coarse face, large tongue, hirsutism + cloudy corneas + stiff joints, umbilical hernia + hepatosplenomegaly + developmental regression + thick ribs, beaked vertebrae + urine glycosaminoglycans up + normal TSH and plasma lysosomal enzymes
highlight: plasma lysosomal enzyme levels are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A lysosomal storage disease. The clincher: **coarse face + clouded corneas + hepatosplenomegaly + skeletal changes + developmental regression, with glycosaminoglycans in the urine**.

nodes.q: Which organelle is affected?
nodes.note: A lysosomal enzyme is missing, so its substrate cannot be broken down and piles up inside the organelle.

nodes.q: Which enzyme is deficient?
nodes.note: Heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate (glycosaminoglycans) build up and spill into the urine. Autosomal recessive. Confirmed by an enzyme assay in white blood cells or fibroblasts.

nodes.q: What is the name for the skeletal changes on his x-rays?
nodes.note: Thickened ribs, beaked vertebrae and short thick bones.

nodes.q: Which treatment slows the brain disease if given early?
nodes.note: Enzyme replacement with laronidase helps the body but does not cross the blood-brain barrier.

nodes.q: His coarse face could suggest Hunter syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **X-linked recessive (boys only), no corneal clouding, aggressive behavior; iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency**
**Autosomal recessive + corneal clouding + dysostosis multiplex**; alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency

nodes.note: The trap: both give coarse features, hepatosplenomegaly and glycosaminoglycans in the urine. Hunter syndrome spares the cornea.

nodes.q: His coarse face could suggest I-cell disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hurler-like, with gum overgrowth and high plasma lysosomal enzymes; no mannose-6-phosphate tagging; normal urine glycosaminoglycans**
**Raised urine glycosaminoglycans + normal plasma lysosomal enzymes + clouded corneas**

nodes.q: His enlarged liver and spleen could suggest Gaucher disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hepatosplenomegaly + bone pain + crumpled-tissue-paper macrophages**; normal face and corneas
**Coarse face + corneal clouding + dysostosis multiplex**

nodes.q: His coarse face and umbilical hernia could suggest congenital hypothyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High thyroid-stimulating hormone + low thyroxine + constipation, prolonged jaundice**; no clouded corneas or enzyme deficiency
**Normal thyroid tests + clouded corneas + urine glycosaminoglycans**

root.stem: A 16-year-old boy has moderate intellectual disability, avoids eye contact, and flaps his hands when excited. He has a long face, large prominent ears, a prominent chin, and a large head for his age. His testes are enlarged, and a mid-systolic click is heard at the apex. His mother has a mild learning disability, and her brother has intellectual disability. His healthy 12-year-old sister has met all milestones and her parents ask whether she should be tested.
root.oneliner: 16M + moderate intellectual disability + avoids eye contact, hand flapping + long face, large prominent ears, prominent chin, large head + enlarged testes + mid-systolic click + mother with mild learning disability + mother's brother with intellectual disability + healthy 12-year-old sister
highlight: mother has a mild learning disability

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. The clincher: **intellectual disability + long face, large ears and enlarged testes after puberty + affected male relatives on the mother's side**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which kind of mutation causes it?
nodes.a: A trinucleotide repeat expansion on the X chromosome
nodes.note: The cytosine-guanine-guanine (CGG) triplet is repeated more than 200 times in the 5' untranslated region of the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) gene. Normal is fewer than about 45 repeats; 55 to 200 is a premutation. Huntington disease is another repeat-expansion disorder.

nodes.q: With more than 200 repeats, what happens to transcription of the gene?
nodes.a: It decreases: the repeats and the promoter become hypermethylated and the gene is silenced
nodes.note: No FMR1 protein is made. That protein normally restrains protein synthesis at synapses, so its loss causes the intellectual disability and the autism-like behavior.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern explains an affected brother of his mother?
nodes.note: Affected males pass the gene through carrier daughters, so it travels down the mother's side.

nodes.q: His mother carries the expanded gene but is only mildly affected. Which process explains her milder disease?
nodes.note: In each of her cells one X is switched off at random, so many cells still use the normal FMR1 copy. Boys have only one X, so every cell lacks the protein.

nodes.q: His mother carries a smaller expansion than he does. Which mechanism makes her children's repeat larger than hers?
nodes.a: Anticipation: the repeat expands further when it is passed on through the egg
nodes.note: Expansion happens during egg formation (maternal meiosis), so each generation is more severely affected. This is why the mother's children are affected more than she is.

nodes.q: Which ovarian disorder occurs in women who carry a premutation (55 to 200 repeats)?
nodes.note: Early menopause before age 40. Called fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency.

nodes.q: Which late-onset neurologic disorder appears after age 50 in men who carry a premutation?
nodes.note: Intention tremor, gait ataxia and cognitive decline.

nodes.q: When do the enlarged testes appear?
nodes.note: Not in early childhood, so a young boy can have the other features without large testes.

nodes.q: Which heart valve finding fits his mid-systolic click?
nodes.note: Connective tissue weakness also explains the joint hypermobility, flat feet and soft skin that can accompany the syndrome.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Molecular genetic testing that counts the CGG repeats in FMR1
nodes.note: Southern blot or methylation-specific analysis shows the full mutation and its methylation. The karyotype is normal; the older fragile site on culture is no longer used.

nodes.q: His parents ask whether his healthy 12-year-old sister should have carrier testing now. What is the most appropriate advice?
nodes.a: Wait until she is older and mature enough to decide for herself
nodes.note: Carrier testing of a healthy child gives no medical benefit in childhood and takes away her own choice. Defer it until she can decide, with genetic counseling, ideally before she plans a family. Testing now is right only if the result would change her care in childhood.

nodes.q: His enlarged testes could suggest Klinefelter syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Tall, long-legged, **small firm testes** (47,XXY), gynecomastia, infertility; learning problems are mild
Long face, large ears, **large testes after puberty**, normal karyotype, repeat expansion in FMR1

nodes.note: The trap: both are sex-chromosome-related boys with learning problems, and both can have a tall or long-faced look.

nodes.q: His intellectual disability could suggest Down syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Flat face, upslanting eyes, **single palmar crease**, heart septal defects; extra chromosome 21 on the karyotype
**Long face, large ears**, prominent chin, mitral valve prolapse; normal karyotype

nodes.q: His hand movements could suggest Rett syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Girls, normal development for 6 to 18 months, then loss of speech and skills with **hand wringing**; mutation in the X-linked methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene
Mostly boys, delayed from the start, **hand flapping with gaze avoidance**, long face, large testes

root.stem: A newborn boy is delivered at 38 weeks after a pregnancy in which ultrasound showed very little amniotic fluid. He has a flattened face with a broad flat nose, a skin fold under each eye, low-set ears, a receding chin, and bilateral clubfeet. He gasps and breathes poorly despite ventilation, and a chest x-ray shows small lungs. He passes no urine, and ultrasound shows no kidneys.
root.oneliner: Newborn boy + very little amniotic fluid + flat face, flat nose, skin fold under each eye, low-set ears, receding chin + bilateral clubfeet + respiratory failure with small lungs + no urine + no kidneys on ultrasound
highlight: flattened face with a broad flat nose

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: One defect (no fetal urine) triggers a chain of others. The clincher: **too little amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios) + flat face and clubfeet + lung failure at birth + absent kidneys**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Also called Potter syndrome; the flat face is called Potter facies.

nodes.q: His kidneys never formed. Which embryonic structure failed to grow out and induce the metanephric mesenchyme?
nodes.note: Without the ureteric bud (from the mesonephric duct) the metanephros never forms: bilateral renal agenesis, the classic start of the sequence. Anything that stops fetal urine can do the same: dysplastic or cystic kidneys, autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, or posterior urethral valves.

nodes.q: Why is there too little amniotic fluid?
nodes.a: The fetus makes no urine, and fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid in the second half of pregnancy
nodes.note: Without fluid, the uterine wall presses directly on the fetus.

nodes.q: Which type of birth defect are the flat face and clubfeet?
nodes.note: Outside compression bends a normally formed body part. A malformation is an intrinsic defect in the tissue itself (here, the kidney agenesis); a disruption is breakdown of normal tissue, for example by amniotic bands.

nodes.q: Which complication kills the newborn?
nodes.note: Small, underdeveloped lungs cannot oxygenate the blood.

nodes.q: Why do the lungs fail to grow?
nodes.a: The fetus cannot breathe in and swallow enough amniotic fluid, and the stretch of fluid is needed for lung growth
nodes.note: The chest is also compressed by the tight uterus.

nodes.q: Which air-leak complication is common in these stiff, hypoplastic lungs on a ventilator?
nodes.note: High pressures rupture the alveoli.

nodes.q: How is it suspected before birth?
nodes.a: Prenatal ultrasound showing an amniotic fluid index below 5 cm with absent kidneys and a bladder that never fills
nodes.note: Death usually follows soon after birth from respiratory failure.

nodes.q: His breathing failure could suggest neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Preterm** infant, normal amniotic fluid and kidneys, ground-glass lungs from **surfactant deficiency**; treated with surfactant
**Term infant, no urine, oligohydramnios, small lungs, flat face**; surfactant does not fix the hypoplasia

nodes.note: The trap: both present with respiratory failure in the first hours.

nodes.q: His small lungs could suggest congenital diaphragmatic hernia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Scaphoid abdomen, **bowel sounds in the chest**, heart shifted away from the hernia; amniotic fluid and kidneys are normal
**Little amniotic fluid, no kidneys, clubfeet and flat face**; normal diaphragm

root.stem: A 24-year-old man has had 1 year of weakness of his thigh muscles and muscle pain after vigorous exercise. His mother, his mother's sister and his maternal grandmother have the same problem, but his father's sister and her children are healthy. Blood lactate rises sharply after mild exercise, and creatine kinase is mildly raised. A quadriceps biopsy stained with Gomori trichrome shows fibers with red, ragged-looking rims.
root.oneliner: 24M + 1 year of thigh weakness + pain after vigorous exercise + mother, maternal aunt and maternal grandmother affected, paternal relatives healthy + lactate rises sharply after mild exercise + mildly raised creatine kinase + biopsy with red, ragged-looking fiber rims
highlight: His mother, his mother's sister and his maternal grandmother
his father's sister and her children are healthy
Blood lactate rises sharply after mild exercise

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A muscle disease from defective mitochondrial DNA. The clincher: **ragged red fibers on biopsy + exercise weakness + inheritance only through the mother**.

nodes.q: Which biopsy finding gives the disease its signature?
nodes.note: Gomori trichrome stains clumps of abnormal mitochondria red under the muscle fiber membrane (subsarcolemmal).

nodes.q: Which inclusion does electron microscopy show inside the abnormal fibers?
nodes.note: The mitochondria are swollen and packed together, with rectangular crystalline inclusions.

nodes.q: In which cell organelle is the mutated gene located?
nodes.note: It has its own circular DNA. Mutations are typically in transfer RNA genes or genes for the respiratory chain.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern explains the affected mother's side only?
nodes.note: Mitochondria come from the egg; sperm mitochondria are lost. An affected mother can pass it to all her children, an affected father to none.

nodes.q: Which phenomenon explains why relatives with the same mutation range from healthy to very weak?
nodes.note: A cell holds a mix of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA; symptoms appear only above a threshold, and the mix is random at each cell division.

nodes.q: Which process is impaired?
nodes.note: Little adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is made, so tissues with high energy demand (muscle, brain, heart) are hit first.

nodes.q: Why does lactate rise after only mild exercise?
nodes.a: The muscle falls back on anaerobic glycolysis, which makes lactate
nodes.note: Pyruvate cannot be burned in the mitochondria, so it is converted to lactate.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the mutation?
nodes.a: Mitochondrial DNA genetic testing (on muscle tissue)
nodes.note: The biopsy has already shown ragged red fibers and can show respiratory-chain enzyme defects; sequencing finds the mutation. Muscle is tested because blood may carry a low mutant load (heteroplasmy).

nodes.q: What care is offered?
nodes.a: Supportive: graded exercise, and coenzyme Q10 and other cofactors are often tried
nodes.note: There is no cure; the evidence for supplements is limited. Avoid mitochondrial toxins such as valproate.

nodes.q: His pain after exercise could suggest McArdle disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Autosomal recessive myophosphorylase deficiency; cramps, **second-wind phenomenon**, dark urine from myoglobin; **lactate does not rise** and glycogen vacuoles are seen
**Maternal inheritance, ragged red fibers, lactate rises sharply** after mild exercise

nodes.note: The trap: both cause exercise-induced muscle pain.

nodes.q: His thigh weakness could suggest Duchenne muscular dystrophy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Young boys, **calf pseudohypertrophy, Gowers sign**, very high creatine kinase; X-linked dystrophin deficiency, so no father-to-son transmission and no affected women
Onset in a young adult, **affected women and men through the mother**, ragged red fibers, only mildly raised creatine kinase

nodes.q: His proximal weakness could suggest polymyositis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Adults without family history, **very high creatine kinase**, endomysial CD8 T cells invading fibers; improves with steroids
**Family history through the mother**, ragged red fibers, lactate rise; no inflammation

nodes.q: His ragged red fibers could also fit myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF). How do you tell them apart?

split.a: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF)
split.note: Same maternal inheritance and ragged red fibers, plus **myoclonic jerks, seizures and ataxia**; usually a transfer RNA-lysine mutation
**Weakness and exercise intolerance only**; no seizures, jerks or stroke-like episodes

nodes.note: Mitochondrial disorders form a family; the brain signs name the syndrome (stroke-like episodes point to MELAS, mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes).

root.stem: A 40-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, has chorionic villus sampling at 11 weeks because of her age. Of the 39 cells counted, 14 have a 46,XY karyotype and 25 have 47,XY,+15. She then has amniocentesis at 16 weeks, and all 50 cells examined are 46,XY. Ultrasound shows normal fetal anatomy, but the fetus measures slightly small for dates.
root.oneliner: 40F + chorionic villus sampling at 11 weeks for age + 25 of 39 villus cells 47,XY,+15 and 14 cells 46,XY + amniocentesis at 16 weeks all 50 cells 46,XY + normal anatomy, slightly small for dates

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The abnormal cell line is in the placenta but not in the fetus. The clincher: **trisomy in many chorionic villus cells + a normal karyotype in amniotic fluid**.

nodes.q: Why can the two samples disagree?
nodes.a: They sample different lineages: villi come from the placenta (trophoblast), while amniotic fluid cells come from the fetus
nodes.note: The placenta and the fetus separate early from different cells of the embryo, so a chromosome error can stay in one lineage.

nodes.q: How does the normal fetal line usually arise?
nodes.a: Trisomy rescue: a trisomic embryo loses the extra chromosome in the cells that form the fetus
nodes.note: The trisomy remains in the placental cells. This usually starts with a maternal meiotic error, which becomes more common with maternal age; less often a mitotic error arises in the placenta alone.

nodes.q: Which fetal problem can follow even with a normal fetal karyotype?
nodes.a: Fetal growth restriction from placental insufficiency
nodes.note: The abnormal placenta works poorly, so the fetus is small for dates. Serial growth ultrasounds follow it.

nodes.q: Which additional test is needed after rescue of a trisomy 15 fetus?
nodes.a: Testing for uniparental disomy of chromosome 15
nodes.note: If the lost chromosome was the paternal one, the fetus keeps two maternal copies.

nodes.q: Which syndrome results if both chromosome 15 copies are maternal?
nodes.note: The paternal 15q11-q13 genes are missing, and the maternal copies are imprinted (silenced).

nodes.q: The trisomy cells could suggest true fetal mosaicism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: The abnormal line is also found in **amniotic fluid or fetal blood**, and the fetus may be affected
**Abnormal cells only in the villi; amniotic fluid normal**

nodes.note: The trap: both show a mix of normal and trisomic cells on the first sample.

nodes.q: The mix of normal and trisomic cells could suggest pseudomosaicism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: A **single abnormal cell or one culture flask**, a culture artifact; not seen in other cultures
**Many abnormal cells (25 of 39), found across the sample**, a real placental cell line

nodes.q: The two results could suggest sample contamination. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Cells with a **different sex or karyotype** from the fetus (for example 46,XX maternal cells) or mislabeled samples
**All cells are XY**; the abnormal line is the same male with an extra chromosome 15

root.stem: An 18-month-old girl is brought for follow-up. She weighed 4.2 kg at birth, needed glucose infusions for low blood sugar in her first days, and had a defect of the abdominal wall at the umbilicus repaired at birth. She remains above the 95th percentile for height and weight. She has a large tongue, a pink patch on her forehead, and her right leg is longer than her left. Both irises look normal. Abdominal ultrasound shows a mass in the left kidney. Genetic testing shows abnormal methylation of the maternal copy of chromosome 11p15.
root.oneliner: 18F + birth weight 4.2 kg, above the 95th percentile + neonatal hypoglycemia + repaired abdominal wall defect + large tongue + forehead pink patch + longer right leg + normal irises + left renal mass + abnormal methylation of maternal 11p15
highlight: abnormal methylation of the maternal copy of chromosome 11p15

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An overgrowth syndrome. The clincher: **overgrowth + large tongue + abdominal wall defect + neonatal hypoglycemia + embryonal tumor**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The three words describe the main features.

nodes.q: Which genetic mechanism causes it?
nodes.note: Most often the maternal imprinting center 2 loses its methylation, which silences the growth suppressor cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1C (CDKN1C). Less often imprinting center 1 gains methylation, so insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2), normally made only from the paternal copy, is made from both copies. Paternal uniparental disomy of 11p15 does both.

nodes.q: Which tumor is her left kidney mass most likely to be?
nodes.note: Also at risk of hepatoblastoma, so screening is essential. Biopsy shows blastema, epithelial tubules and stroma.

nodes.q: How are children screened for these tumors?
nodes.a: Abdominal ultrasound every 3 months until about age 7, plus serum alpha-fetoprotein every 3 months until about age 4
nodes.note: Alpha-fetoprotein detects hepatoblastoma.

nodes.q: Why was her blood sugar low after birth?
nodes.note: The overgrowth includes the pancreatic islets, so the newborn makes too much insulin. It usually settles within weeks.

nodes.q: Which abdominal wall defect is typical?
nodes.note: Bowel or liver herniates into a sac at the umbilicus, covered by membrane.

nodes.q: What is the name for the one-sided overgrowth that made her right leg longer?
nodes.note: It also marks a higher risk of embryonal tumors.

nodes.q: Her kidney mass could suggest WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, range of intellectual disability). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Wilms tumor, **absent irises (aniridia)**, genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability; deletion at 11p13 of the Wilms tumor 1 (WT1) and paired box 6 (PAX6) genes, **not overgrown**
**Overgrowth, large tongue, hemihyperplasia, normal irises**; imprinting defect at 11p15

nodes.note: The trap: both involve Wilms tumor and chromosome 11.

nodes.q: Her overgrowth could suggest Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: X-linked loss of glypican 3 (GPC3), mostly boys; **extra nipples, polydactyly, coarse face**, overgrowth
**Large tongue, omphalocele, hemihyperplasia**, girls as often as boys; imprinting at 11p15

nodes.q: The imprinting error could suggest Prader-Willi syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Loss of **paternal** 15q11-q13; floppy newborn, then **obesity from constant hunger**, short stature, small genitalia
Abnormal **maternal** 11p15 methylation; **overgrowth** and tumors
