root.stem: A 7-month-old boy of Ashkenazi Jewish descent is brought because he has stopped rolling over and sitting, which he did at 5 months. He startles strongly at ordinary noises, has poor head control, and does not follow faces. Eye examination shows a bright red spot at the center of each macula with a pale white retina around it. The liver and spleen are not enlarged.
root.oneliner: 7M + Ashkenazi Jewish + lost sitting and rolling + exaggerated startle to noise + floppy, poor head control + red spot in each macula with pale retina + normal liver and spleen
highlight: bright red spot at the center of each macula

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A lysosomal storage disease of neurons. The clincher: **loss of milestones in infancy + exaggerated startle + cherry-red macula + no enlarged liver or spleen (hepatosplenomegaly) + Ashkenazi Jewish descent**.

nodes.q: Which lysosomal enzyme is missing?
nodes.note: It removes N-acetylgalactosamine from GM2 ganglioside. The gene (HEXA) is on chromosome 15.

nodes.q: Which substance builds up in neurons?
nodes.note: Lysosomes fill with concentric lamellae that look like onion skin on electron microscopy, and the neurons swell. Tay-Sachs is the classic GM2 gangliosidosis.

nodes.q: Which retinal structure looks cherry-red?
nodes.note: The surrounding ganglion cells are swollen and pale from stored ganglioside; the thin fovea has none, so the choroid shows through as red.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern does it follow?
nodes.note: Both parents are healthy carriers.

nodes.q: In a population where the disease affects 1 in 3600, what is the carrier frequency?
nodes.note: Hardy-Weinberg: q squared = 1/3600, so q = 1/60. Carriers are 2pq, which is nearly 2q = 1/30.

nodes.q: Which type of mutation is the most common in Ashkenazi Jewish carriers?
nodes.a: A frameshift mutation (a 4-base-pair insertion in HEXA)
nodes.note: The shifted reading frame produces an early stop codon, so no working enzyme is made.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Low hexosaminidase A activity in serum or leukocytes
nodes.note: Carriers can be found with the same test or by HEXA genetic testing.

nodes.q: What is the outcome?
nodes.a: Relentless neurodegeneration with death in early childhood
nodes.note: Seizures, blindness and decerebration follow; there is no cure, so care is supportive, with genetic counseling and carrier screening in at-risk populations.

nodes.q: His cherry-red macula could suggest Niemann-Pick disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hepatosplenomegaly**, foamy macrophages; sphingomyelinase deficiency
**No hepatosplenomegaly**, hexosaminidase A deficiency, onion-skin lysosomes

nodes.note: The trap: both show a cherry-red macula and neurodegeneration in Ashkenazi infants.

nodes.q: His Ashkenazi ancestry could suggest Gaucher disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Enlarged liver and spleen, **bone pain, Erlenmeyer flask deformity**, crumpled-tissue-paper macrophages; glucocerebrosidase deficiency, no cherry-red spot
**Infant regression with cherry-red macula**, normal organs

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching picture of a fully dressed infant lying on a play mat, unable to sit up, with a magnified retina beside him showing a bright red spot at the macula surrounded by pale retina; no text.

root.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought for poor growth and developmental delay. She has coarse facial features, thickened gums, stiff joints that cannot fully extend, and a dislocated hip. Radiographs show thickened, paddle-shaped ribs, beaked vertebral bodies and short, broad hand bones. Blood tests show markedly raised activities of several lysosomal enzymes in her plasma, and a urine test shows no excess mucopolysaccharides. Cultured skin fibroblasts contain many dense inclusions in the cytoplasm. She has no cherry-red spot in the eye, no bone pain, and her spleen is not enlarged.
root.oneliner: 2F + poor growth and developmental delay + coarse face, thick gums, stiff joints, hip dislocation + paddle-shaped ribs, beaked vertebrae, short broad hand bones + high plasma lysosomal enzymes + normal urine mucopolysaccharides + dense inclusions in fibroblasts + no cherry-red spot, no bone pain, no splenomegaly
highlight: markedly raised activities of several lysosomal enzymes in her plasma

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A lysosomal disease in which the enzymes are made but never reach the lysosome. The clincher: **coarse features and bone changes of a storage disease with high lysosomal enzymes in plasma and normal urine mucopolysaccharides**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease; exam stems often write 'mucolipidosis II (I-cell disease)'.

nodes.q: Which blood result separates it from most other storage diseases?
nodes.a: High lysosomal enzyme activity in plasma
nodes.note: In most storage diseases one enzyme is low. Here many enzymes leak out of cells, so plasma levels are high and the lysosomes are empty of them.

nodes.q: Which step of lysosomal enzyme processing fails?
nodes.a: Addition of phosphate to mannose residues (forming mannose 6-phosphate) in the cis-Golgi
nodes.note: The missing enzyme is N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase (phosphotransferase). Synthesis and N-linked glycosylation of the enzymes are normal; only the phosphorylated tag is absent. Autosomal recessive (GNPTAB gene).

nodes.q: What happens to the newly made lysosomal enzymes?
nodes.a: They are mis-targeted and leave the cell by the default secretory route instead of reaching lysosomes
nodes.note: The mannose 6-phosphate receptor in the trans-Golgi cannot bind them, so they are secreted into the blood. That is why plasma levels rise and the lysosomes fill with undigested material.

nodes.q: What fills the dense inclusions in her cultured fibroblasts?
nodes.a: Undigested oligosaccharides, lipids and glycosaminoglycans inside lysosomes that lack their enzymes
nodes.note: These inclusions (I) give the disease its name. Some cells, such as hepatocytes, use a mannose 6-phosphate-independent route and keep near-normal lysosomal enzymes.

nodes.q: What is the name for her pattern of rib, vertebral and hand bone changes on radiographs?
nodes.note: Paddle-shaped ribs, beaked vertebrae and short, broad bones, with joint contractures and hip dislocation. It shows defective bone and cartilage turnover and also occurs in the mucopolysaccharidoses.

nodes.q: What is the usual outcome?
nodes.a: Death in early childhood, often from heart and lung failure
nodes.note: Most children die in the first decade, usually by about 5 to 7 years. There is no cure; bone marrow transplantation has not helped much.

nodes.q: Which test confirms it?
nodes.a: Low N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase activity in cultured fibroblasts, confirmed by GNPTAB gene testing
nodes.note: Raised plasma lysosomal enzymes point to it first. Genetic testing also allows carrier detection and prenatal diagnosis.

nodes.q: Her coarse face and bone changes could suggest Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type I). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Corneal clouding + hepatosplenomegaly + excess dermatan and heparan sulfate in urine**; alpha-L-iduronidase is low and plasma enzymes are normal
**Normal urine mucopolysaccharides + high plasma lysosomal enzymes + dense inclusions in fibroblasts**; thickened gums and joint contractures from infancy

nodes.note: The trap: both give a coarse face, joint stiffness and the same radiographic bone changes.

nodes.q: Other storage diseases were also possible. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: Each has a different clincher.

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from her case
rows: Hunter syndrome
**X-linked boys with excess dermatan and heparan sulfate in urine; iduronate sulfatase deficiency**
She is a girl with normal urine mucopolysaccharides
Tay-Sachs disease
**Cherry-red macular spot + hyperacusis + hexosaminidase A deficiency**; no coarse face
No cherry-red spot and she has coarse features
Gaucher disease
**Hepatosplenomegaly + bone pain + wrinkled-paper macrophages; glucocerebrosidase deficiency**
No spleen enlargement or bone pain

root.stem: A 10-year-old girl is seen because of seven flat, evenly light brown spots on her trunk, each 1 to 3 cm wide. Freckling is seen in both armpits, and a slit-lamp examination shows tiny pigmented bumps on both irises. Her mother has two soft skin nodules and similar spots, while her maternal uncle has hundreds of skin nodules covering his body. Her hearing and vision are normal and her neurologic examination is normal. She has had no seizures, no nosebleeds, no white leaf-shaped patches, no facial bumps, and no unusual or irregular moles.
root.oneliner: 10F + 7 flat, evenly light brown spots 1-3 cm + axillary freckling + pigmented iris bumps + mother with 2 skin nodules, uncle with hundreds + normal hearing, vision and neurologic exam + no seizures, nosebleeds, white leaf-shaped patches, facial bumps or irregular moles
highlight: seven flat, evenly light brown spots
Freckling is seen in both armpits
tiny pigmented bumps on both irises
mother has two soft skin nodules
maternal uncle has hundreds of skin nodules

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disease. The clincher: **six or more café-au-lait macules (flat, evenly light brown spots) plus axillary freckling**, with pigmented iris bumps and an affected parent.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Also called peripheral neurofibromatosis; the exam may write only 'neurofibromatosis'.

nodes.q: How many café-au-lait macules over 5 mm are needed before puberty to count toward the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The diagnosis needs two or more of seven features: six or more café-au-lait macules, two or more neurofibromas (or one plexiform), axillary or groin freckling, optic pathway glioma, two or more iris hamartomas, a characteristic bone lesion (such as sphenoid wing dysplasia or tibial bowing), or an affected parent. She has seven spots, freckling, iris bumps and an affected mother.

nodes.q: Which tumor suppressor gene is mutated?
nodes.a: The NF1 gene on chromosome 17, which encodes neurofibromin
nodes.note: Germline loss of one copy; the tumors arise when the second copy is lost.

nodes.q: What does neurofibromin normally do?
nodes.a: Turns off Ras (it is a GTPase-activating protein)
nodes.note: Without it, Ras stays active and cell growth signalling through the MAP kinase pathway is unchecked.

nodes.q: How is it inherited?
nodes.a: Autosomal dominant, with about half of cases due to new mutations
nodes.note: Complete penetrance: everyone with the mutation shows some feature by adulthood.

nodes.q: Which term describes the mild disease in her mother and the severe disease in her uncle from the same mutation?
nodes.note: Penetrance is the chance of showing any sign; expressivity is how severe the signs are in those who do.

nodes.q: What are the pigmented iris bumps called?
nodes.note: Benign iris hamartomas that appear from about age 6 and do not harm vision.

nodes.q: Which benign nerve sheath tumors appear on the skin in adolescence?
nodes.note: Soft, skin-colored nodules made of Schwann cells, fibroblasts and mast cells; the Schwann cells come from the neural crest.

nodes.q: Which cancer may develop from a deep plexiform neurofibroma?
nodes.note: Suspect it when a known plexiform tumor grows quickly or becomes painful.

nodes.q: Which childhood brain tumor of the visual pathway is typical?
nodes.note: Present in about 15 percent; may cause vision loss or early puberty.

nodes.q: Which test is done every year in a child to look for it?
nodes.note: Also check blood pressure (renal artery stenosis or pheochromocytoma) and the spine for scoliosis. Magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for symptoms.

nodes.q: If she later develops episodes of high blood pressure, sweating and headache, which adrenal tumor should be suspected?
nodes.note: A classic association; neurofibromatosis type 1 also raises the risk of renal artery stenosis.

nodes.q: Selumetinib shrinks inoperable plexiform neurofibromas in children. Which kinase downstream of Ras does it block?
nodes.note: With neurofibromin lost, Ras keeps signalling through RAF, MEK and ERK; blocking MEK slows tumor growth. Otherwise management is surveillance and surgery for symptomatic tumors.

nodes.q: Her skin spots and family history could suggest tuberous sclerosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Ash-leaf (white) macules + facial angiofibromas + seizures or infantile spasms**; cortical tubers, cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma
**Café-au-lait macules + axillary freckling + Lisch nodules + neurofibromas**; no seizures or white patches

nodes.note: The trap: both are autosomal dominant neurocutaneous diseases with skin spots.

nodes.q: Other conditions were also possible. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: Each has a different clincher.

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from her case
rows: Neurofibromatosis type 2
**Bilateral vestibular schwannomas with hearing loss, tinnitus and unsteadiness**; few skin spots
Her hearing is normal and she has axillary freckling
Von Hippel-Lindau disease
**Retinal and cerebellar hemangioblastomas + renal cell carcinoma**
No tumors of the retina or cerebellum; spots are café-au-lait
Osler-Weber-Rendu disease
**Recurrent nosebleeds + mucocutaneous telangiectasias + arteriovenous malformations**
No nosebleeds; spots are flat and evenly brown
Dysplastic nevus syndrome
**Many irregular, variably pigmented moles with a family history of melanoma**
Her spots are uniform; no irregular moles

root.stem: A 6-month-old boy of Ashkenazi Jewish descent is brought because of poor feeding and repeated vomiting since early infancy. He is floppy and has lost skills he had gained, such as holding up his head. His liver and spleen are enlarged. An eye examination shows a cherry-red spot at the macula, and a bone marrow biopsy shows many large macrophages with foamy cytoplasm. He has no skin rash, no limb pain and no bone pain, and he does not startle to loud noise.
root.oneliner: 6M, Ashkenazi Jewish + poor feeding and vomiting from early infancy + hypotonia and loss of skills + hepatosplenomegaly + cherry-red macular spot + foamy macrophages in marrow + no rash, no limb or bone pain, no startle to noise
highlight: does not startle to loud noise

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A lysosomal storage disease of sphingomyelin. The clincher: **hepatosplenomegaly + loss of skills + cherry-red macular spot in an Ashkenazi Jewish infant**. Type A is the severe infantile form, with the highest carrier rate in Ashkenazi Jews; type B has organ disease without brain disease.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which metabolic pathway is blocked?
nodes.a: Degradation of sphingomyelin in the lysosome
nodes.note: The lysosomal hydrolase acid sphingomyelinase is low, so sphingomyelin is not split into ceramide and phosphorylcholine. The problem is decreased lysosomal breakdown, not increased synthesis or diet. Autosomal recessive (SMPD1 gene).

nodes.q: What do the lysosomes of his foamy macrophages look like on electron microscopy?
nodes.note: The stored sphingomyelin forms layered membrane whorls. The lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) crowd the marrow, liver, spleen and lymph nodes.

nodes.q: Why does his macula look cherry-red?
nodes.a: Lipid-filled retinal ganglion cells make the surrounding retina pale, while the fovea, which has no ganglion cells, shows the red choroid beneath
nodes.note: Tay-Sachs disease shows the same spot for the same reason.

nodes.q: What is the usual outcome of the infantile form?
nodes.a: Death by about 2 to 3 years of age
nodes.note: There is progressive loss of motor and mental skills.

nodes.q: Which form is caused by defective lysosomal cholesterol transport rather than by an enzyme deficiency?
nodes.note: NPC1 gene mutation. Look for vertical gaze palsy, ataxia and cataplexy; treated with miglustat.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Low sphingomyelinase activity in white blood cells or fibroblasts, with SMPD1 gene testing
nodes.note: Marrow foam cells are suggestive but not specific.

nodes.q: Which enzyme replacement therapy treats the non-brain manifestations?
nodes.note: It does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so it does not help the infantile neurologic disease; care is otherwise supportive.

root.stem: A 24-year-old lean man comes to the emergency department with 8 hours of severe upper abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. He had similar episodes in childhood, and his brother also had pancreatitis. He takes no medications and drinks no alcohol. Crops of yellow-red bumps are on his trunk and buttocks, and his retinal vessels look creamy white. His blood is milky with a triglyceride level of 3500 mg/dL, glucose 90 mg/dL, and lipase 400 U/L. After refrigeration overnight, the plasma shows a creamy top layer over a clear fluid below. Triglyceride-splitting activity in his plasma after a heparin injection is very low and does not rise when normal plasma is added. He has no tendon xanthomas, no yellow palm creases and no family history of early heart attacks.
root.oneliner: 24M, lean + severe epigastric pain with vomiting, similar childhood episodes, brother with pancreatitis + no drugs or alcohol + crops of yellow-red bumps on trunk and buttocks + creamy-white retinal vessels + milky blood, triglycerides 3500, lipase 400, normal glucose + creamy top layer on refrigeration + very low post-heparin triglyceride-splitting activity, not corrected by normal plasma + no tendon xanthomas, palm creases or early heart attacks in the family
highlight: takes no medications and drinks no alcohol
creamy top layer over a clear fluid below
does not rise when normal plasma is added
no family history of early heart attacks

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A genetic failure to clear dietary fat particles from the blood. The clincher: **milky blood with triglycerides in the thousands and a creamy top layer on standing, with attacks since childhood**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease; the exam may also call it type I familial dyslipidemia.

nodes.q: The creamy top layer is made of particles built in the intestine. Which apolipoprotein is unique to them?
nodes.note: Chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride and are the largest, lightest lipoproteins, so they float to the top on standing and leave clear plasma below. Excess very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), which carries apolipoprotein B-100, gives uniform cloudiness instead.

nodes.q: Which enzyme fails to break down the triglycerides in chylomicrons?
nodes.note: The enzyme sits on capillary endothelium and needs apolipoprotein C-II as its activator. Mutations in the enzyme itself are most common; defects in apolipoprotein C-II or in the proteins that anchor it (GPIHBP1) give the same picture. Autosomal recessive. Hormone-sensitive lipase is a different enzyme: it breaks down stored fat inside adipocytes, not circulating particles.

nodes.q: Which skin lesions appear in crops when triglycerides are this high?
nodes.note: Lipid-filled foam cells in the dermis; they fade within weeks of lowering triglycerides.

nodes.q: What is the creamy-white appearance of his retinal vessels called?
nodes.note: It disappears when triglycerides fall.

nodes.q: Which dangerous complication of the high triglycerides brought him in?
nodes.note: Risk rises sharply when triglycerides exceed 1000 mg/dL. Lipase is raised and glucose is normal.

nodes.q: How do the lipids injure the pancreas?
nodes.a: Pancreatic lipase splits triglycerides into toxic free fatty acids in the pancreatic capillaries
nodes.note: The free fatty acids damage the acinar cells and capillaries, starting the inflammation.

nodes.q: How is a severe attack managed?
nodes.a: Fasting with intravenous fluids, plus insulin infusion or plasmapheresis to bring triglycerides down quickly
nodes.note: Stop any triglyceride-raising drugs. Lipase and amylase may be falsely normal when blood is this lipemic.

nodes.q: Which dietary change lowers the risk of attacks?
nodes.a: A very low fat diet, with medium-chain triglycerides for calories
nodes.note: Medium-chain fats are absorbed directly into the portal vein, not packaged into chylomicrons. Fat intake is kept to about 10 to 15 percent of calories.

nodes.q: Which lipid-lowering drug class works by raising lipoprotein lipase activity and so does little for him?
nodes.note: Fibrates activate the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha; they need a working lipase. Newer options lower apolipoprotein C-III (olezarsen).

nodes.q: Why is his risk of early coronary disease not clearly raised?
nodes.a: Chylomicrons are too large to enter the artery wall
nodes.note: Atherosclerosis is mainly driven by smaller low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and remnant particles; pancreatitis is the main danger here.

nodes.q: Apolipoprotein C-II deficiency gives the same milky blood. How do you tell it from his disease?

split.note: **Lipase activity rises when normal plasma (which supplies apolipoprotein C-II) is added**

split.a: Familial chylomicronemia syndrome from lipoprotein lipase deficiency
split.note: **Lipase activity stays very low even when normal plasma is added**

nodes.note: The trap: both give chylomicronemia and pancreatitis from childhood.

nodes.q: Other lipid disorders were also possible. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: Each has a different clincher.

Clincher

**Triglycerides 200 to 1000 mg/dL, cloudy serum, adult onset with obesity or diabetes; excess VLDL**
Triglycerides 3500 with a creamy top layer from childhood, lean

**Very high LDL cholesterol + tendon xanthomas + early heart attacks; LDL receptor defect**
No tendon xanthomas or early heart attacks
Dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III)
**Yellow palm creases + raised cholesterol and triglycerides; apolipoprotein E2/E2**

root.stem: A 31-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. At age 8 she was treated for an adrenocortical carcinoma. Her mother had a soft tissue sarcoma at age 29, her brother died of a glioblastoma at age 17, and a maternal aunt had osteosarcoma at age 24. Testing of the family found no BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation. She had no eye tumor in infancy, and no one in the family has had colon or endometrial cancer.
root.oneliner: 31F + breast cancer + adrenocortical carcinoma at 8 + mother with sarcoma at 29, brother with glioblastoma at 17, aunt with osteosarcoma at 24 + no BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation + no infant eye tumor + no colon or endometrial cancer in the family
highlight: no one in the family has had colon or endometrial cancer

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited cancer syndrome. The clincher: **sarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumor and adrenocortical carcinoma at young ages in several relatives**. Mnemonic SBLA: Sarcoma, Breast and brain, Leukemia, Adrenal gland.

nodes.q: Which tumor suppressor gene carries the germline mutation?
nodes.note: Chromosome 17p. p53 is the 'guardian of the genome'. Autosomal dominant with very high penetrance.

nodes.q: Why do tumors arise in carriers who inherited only one faulty copy?
nodes.a: A cell loses the second, normal copy (the two-hit hypothesis)
nodes.note: Every cell starts with one hit, so a single further somatic hit is enough, which is why cancers appear early and often. Many tumors also carry dominant-negative p53 mutants.

nodes.q: What does p53 do after DNA damage?
nodes.a: It stops the cell cycle for repair and triggers apoptosis if repair fails
nodes.note: It induces p21, which blocks the cyclin-dependent kinases at the G1/S checkpoint, and induces BAX for apoptosis.

nodes.q: His p53 mutation weakens contact with its DNA binding sequence. Which enzyme is then recruited less to the promoters of its growth-inhibiting target genes?
nodes.note: p53 is a transcription factor: it binds its response element near target genes such as p21 and helps assemble the preinitiation complex, so RNA polymerase II binds the promoter (TATA box region). Mutant p53 cannot bind DNA, so less RNA polymerase is recruited and transcription of these growth-inhibiting genes falls. DNA polymerase replicates DNA and is not involved in transcription.

nodes.q: Which protein normally tags p53 for degradation to keep its level low?
nodes.note: DNA damage blocks MDM2 and p53 rises.

nodes.q: Which treatment of the first cancer raises the risk of second cancers and is avoided when possible?
nodes.note: Carriers develop radiation-induced tumors within the field.

nodes.q: Which imaging is preferred for yearly surveillance of carriers?
nodes.note: It replaces radiograph- and CT-based screening to avoid radiation; brain and breast magnetic resonance imaging are also done.

nodes.q: Her breast cancer and family cancers could suggest hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.a: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome
split.note: **Breast and ovarian cancer (also prostate, pancreas) with a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation**
**Sarcoma + adrenocortical carcinoma + brain tumor in the young with a TP53 mutation** and no BRCA mutation

nodes.note: The trap: breast cancer at a young age in both.

nodes.q: Her aunt's osteosarcoma could suggest hereditary retinoblastoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **White pupil (leukocoria) in infancy**, then osteosarcoma and other sarcomas later
**No eye tumor in infancy; breast cancer, brain tumor and adrenocortical carcinoma**

root.stem: A 10-month-old boy, born at 34 weeks, is brought because he has stopped doing things he could do before and has had seizures. He is floppy with poor weight gain. His hair is sparse, brittle, kinky and light in color, and his face has chubby drooping cheeks. His skin is loose, but his joints are not hypermobile. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are low, lysyl oxidase activity is reduced in cultured skin cells, and magnetic resonance imaging shows cerebral atrophy with twisted brain arteries. His urine has no musty odor, his lenses are normal, and a maternal uncle died in infancy with similar hair.
root.oneliner: 10M, born at 34 weeks + lost skills and seizures + hypotonia, poor weight gain + sparse, brittle, kinky, light hair + chubby drooping cheeks + loose skin, non-hypermobile joints + low serum copper and ceruloplasmin + low lysyl oxidase + cerebral atrophy, tortuous arteries + no musty urine, normal lenses + maternal uncle died in infancy
highlight: stopped doing things he could do before
sparse, brittle, kinky and light in color
Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are low

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A copper-transport disease of infant boys. The clincher: **kinky, brittle, pale hair + neurodegeneration with low serum copper and ceruloplasmin**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Kinky hair disease (Menkes kinky hair syndrome)
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which gene is mutated?
nodes.note: Copper is absorbed into the gut cells but cannot be pumped out into the blood, so the brain and other tissues are starved of copper. X-linked recessive, which explains the affected maternal uncle.

nodes.q: His lysyl oxidase activity is low. Which structural protein then fails to be cross-linked, giving loose skin and twisted arteries?
nodes.note: Lysyl oxidase is copper-dependent and cross-links collagen (and elastin). Weak connective tissue gives loose skin, bladder diverticula and tortuous, weak arteries that can form aneurysms. Ceruloplasmin is also low, but only because copper is not delivered to the liver to load it.

nodes.q: Which copper-dependent enzyme of the melanocyte explains the pale hair?
nodes.note: Low tyrosinase activity reduces melanin; the hair is also brittle because of poor keratin cross-linking.

nodes.q: Which copper-dependent mitochondrial enzyme complex fails and adds to the hypotonia and low body temperature?
nodes.note: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase (norepinephrine synthesis) and superoxide dismutase are also copper-dependent.

nodes.q: What is the usual outcome?
nodes.a: Death in early childhood, usually by age 3
nodes.note: Progressive neurodegeneration with seizures, and vascular or bladder complications.

nodes.q: Which hair finding on light microscopy supports the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Pili torti (flattened hair shafts twisted on their own axis)
nodes.note: Low serum copper and ceruloplasmin and ATP7A gene testing confirm it.

nodes.q: Which treatment, started in the first weeks of life, can help?
nodes.note: Oral copper does not work because absorption is the defect. Benefit is greatest if started before neurodegeneration.

nodes.q: His low ceruloplasmin could suggest Wilson disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Copper overload: liver disease, psychiatric symptoms, Kayser-Fleischer rings, high urine copper**; ATP7B mutation, usually in teens
**Copper deficiency in an infant boy: kinky pale hair, seizures, loss of skills**; ATP7A mutation, X-linked

nodes.note: The trap: both are copper-transporting ATPase disorders with low ceruloplasmin.

nodes.q: Other conditions were also possible. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: Each has a different clincher.

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
**Hyperextensible skin and hypermobile joints with easy bruising**; collagen defect
His joints are not hypermobile, and hair and brain disease point elsewhere
Phenylketonuria
**Musty urine odor, fair hair and eczema with intellectual disability; high phenylalanine**
No musty odor and the hair is kinky
Marfan syndrome
**Tall build, lens dislocation, aortic root dilation; fibrillin-1 defect**
Normal lenses and no tall habitus

root.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought because of a 4-day history of stumbling gait, stiff muscles, slurred speech and decreased thinking ability. Blood lactate is high, with a lactate-to-pyruvate ratio of 30 (normal is below 20). Magnetic resonance imaging shows symmetric lesions in the basal ganglia and brainstem. Mitochondria isolated from a muscle biopsy use very little oxygen when given glutamate and malate, but normal amounts when given succinate. She takes no medications.
root.oneliner: 5F + 4 days of stumbling gait, stiff muscles, slurred speech, falling cognition + high lactate, lactate-to-pyruvate ratio 30 + symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions + muscle mitochondria use little oxygen with glutamate and malate but normal with succinate + no medications
highlight: symmetric lesions in the basal ganglia and brainstem
very little oxygen when given glutamate and malate

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common respiratory chain defect in children. The clincher: **mitochondria that cannot oxidize substrates feeding reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) but oxidize succinate (which feeds reduced flavin adenine dinucleotide, FADH2) normally, with lactic acidosis and a high lactate-to-pyruvate ratio**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All names describe the same defect.

nodes.q: What does complex I normally do?
nodes.a: Passes electrons from NADH to coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) while pumping protons out of the matrix
nodes.note: Glutamate and malate feed NADH into complex I. Without it, the NADH-linked oxygen use falls.

nodes.q: Through which complex do electrons from succinate bypass the defect?
nodes.a: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), which passes electrons directly to coenzyme Q
nodes.note: FADH2 never passes through complex I, so succinate oxidation is normal.

nodes.q: Why is her lactate high with a raised lactate-to-pyruvate ratio?
nodes.a: NADH cannot be reoxidized, so pyruvate is converted to lactate
nodes.note: A high NADH/NAD+ ratio pushes lactate dehydrogenase toward lactate.

nodes.q: Which brainstem and basal ganglia disease in children is classically caused by this defect?
nodes.note: Brain regions with high energy demand are damaged first.

nodes.q: How can it be inherited?
nodes.a: Autosomal recessive through nuclear NDUF genes, or maternally through mitochondrial MT-ND genes
nodes.note: Maternal transmission arises because the egg supplies the mitochondria; heteroplasmy explains variable severity.

nodes.q: Which maternally inherited cause of sudden, painless central vision loss in young men is classically due to mutations in mitochondrial complex I genes?
nodes.note: Usually one eye, then the other within weeks to months; mitochondrial DNA mutations in MT-ND genes. Affected men cannot pass it on.

nodes.q: Which insecticide and fish poison blocks the same complex?
nodes.note: The toxin MPP+ (made from the contaminant MPTP) also inhibits complex I and causes parkinsonism; metformin inhibits it weakly.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the defect?
nodes.a: Respiratory chain enzyme analysis in a muscle biopsy, with genetic testing
nodes.note: Blood lactate, pyruvate and the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio screen for respiratory chain disease.

nodes.q: Which commonly used antiseizure drug should be avoided in mitochondrial disease?
nodes.note: It can precipitate liver failure, especially with POLG mutations. Care is supportive; coenzyme Q10 and riboflavin are often tried.

nodes.q: Her lactic acidosis and brain disease could suggest pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lactic acidosis with a normal lactate-to-pyruvate ratio; glutamate- and malate-driven respiration is normal**; a ketogenic diet helps
**High lactate-to-pyruvate ratio (30) + low respiration with glutamate and malate but normal with succinate**

nodes.note: The trap: both give lactic acidosis and neurologic decline in childhood.

nodes.q: Her test compared two routes of electron entry into the chain. How would complex II deficiency differ from her result?

split.note: **Low oxygen use with succinate, normal with glutamate and malate**
**Low with glutamate and malate, normal with succinate**

nodes.q: Other chain defects were also possible. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: Each has a different clincher.

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from her case
rows: Complex III deficiency
**Low oxygen use with both NADH-linked and succinate substrates**; exercise intolerance, lactic acidosis
Her succinate use is normal
Complex IV deficiency
**Low oxygen use with both substrates; cytochrome c oxidase stain reduced in muscle**
Her succinate use is normal

**ATP synthase defect: oxygen use is low with all substrates when coupled to ATP synthesis but recovers with an uncoupler**; neuropathy, ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa (NARP)
Her succinate-driven oxygen use is normal
